cards.body: The U.S. Department of Commerce has added Megaspeed and six affiliated entities to its Entity List due to concerns about diversion of advanced AI accelerators to China. However, unlike previous additions of companies suspected of similar activities, the department did not apply a special foreign direct product rule (FDPR) designation to Megaspeed, which raised questions about the effectiveness of the restrictions. While the omission potentially limits the scope of the sanctions, existing U.S. export controls should still restrict Megaspeed's access to advanced processors from AMD and Nvidia. Former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang , allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset , is the woman at the heart of the Jensen Huang scandal, which saw Nvidia's CEO resign and then be reinstated as head of the company in recent days . Go deeper with TH Premium: Taiwan, trade, and tariffs (Image credit: tsmc) While the U.S. flip-flops on chip sanctions, China is building its own chip supply market The state of China's decade-long semiconductor push Huawei Ascend NPU roadmap examined China's CXMT targets 30% DRAM memory market share by 2030 with sixth mega-fab China's latest round of rare-earth export controls explained Chris McGuire , a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and a former Biden administration official who dealt with export controls at the National Security Council, noted that neither Megaspeed nor any of the six associated entities received a so-called Footnote 4 designation on the Entity List. According to McGuire, the Department of Commerce had previously applied the designation to Chinese companies blacklisted over concerns about their access to advanced AI processors. McGuire claims that without the application of the Entity List-specific FDPR, the new restrictions will have essentially no effect on Megaspeed's ability to procure Nvidia's AI processors since, while they are developed in the U.S., the vast majority of them are produced by TSMC in Taiwan. While McGuire acknowledged that new U.S. export controls that took effect on November 19 already require licenses for shipments of high-end AI accelerators to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil, with exemptions for U.S.-based companies and their subsidiaries (i.e., Google or Microsoft can get Rubin-based machines for their data centers in the said countries, but Megaspeed or other local players cannot), he questioned the rationale behind Megaspeed's addition to the Entity List without Footnote 4. It is necessary to note that the new country-wide controls impose a license requirement, not an outright ban, whereas the addition of Megaspeed to the Entity List subjects license applications to a presumption of denial, which is a reason why the designation has practical effect even without Footnote 4. cards.body: Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that Attorney General Todd Blanche told him Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not under investigation. "I was told by the Department of Justice and multiple officials in our national security apparatus that he was under no investigation," Vance told reporters in Ohio on Wednesday after being asked what assurances he had gotten that Huang was not under investigation. "Not even that he was about to be prosecuted; that he's under no investigation." Vance spoke two days after President Donald Trump told CNBC in an interview that an investigation had been done. Trump was asked what Blanche had told him about potential criminal liability for Huang and the question of whether Nvidia chips had ended up in China in violation of U.S. export laws. "They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he, himself, was exonerated," Trump said Monday. Reuters reported Wednesday that the Department of Justice did not conduct a formal investigation into Huang before Trump pushed for his reinstatement as CEO. Blanche had concluded there was no evidence Huang had broken any laws based on investigations into Nvidia clients Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed, according to the report. The DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Reuters report. And the White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on Vance saying Huang was under no investigation when Trump had said there was one. Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment about Vance's remarks. Blanche on Tuesday dodged questions about whether there had been an investigation. "What the president said is that he talked to a lot of people going into the decision that he made to encourage the board to reinstate him," Blanche said after being asked whether the DOJ had investigated Huang and, if so, what were the results of the probe. Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia on Monday, after the chipmaker's board of directors said it had received "input from senior levels of the United States government" that Huang was not a national security risk. Trump took credit for Huang's reinstatement in the interview with CNBC shortly after Nvidia's announcement. Huang resigned following The New York Times reporting multiple affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who is alleged to be a spy for Beijing and who was an executive for the Singapore-based cloud provider Megaspeed. The reporting added fuel to allegations that Nvidia should have known its artificial intelligence chips were being diverted to China and being used by Chinese companies, violating U.S. export laws. "The product they create is a very important part of us staying ahead of the SI arms race with China. We really do care about ensuring those chips do not fall into the wrong hands," Vance said, using the Trump administration's preferred acronym for AI, which the president calls "super intelligence." cards.body: Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems. Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said. Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule. The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information. The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19. Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people. Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Scrutiny over Chinese access to Nvidia chips Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips. The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC. In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI, of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes." "For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he said. "Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries." cards.body: A former cryptominer is pivoting to AI data center colocation and has secured a new customer for its site in Canada. TSXV-listed Sato Technologies Corp. announced this week that it has signed Datum Technology as its first AI customer at its existing data center and cryptomining facility in Québec. Sato subsidiary Qritical AI and Datum entered into a master services agreement and an initial service order in late October, and handed over the space in November. Full details of the deal haven’t been shared. Under the agreement, Datum has completed an initial deployment of Nvidia B300 (Blackwell Ultra) GPU servers at Sato’s 20MW hydro-powered site in Joliette, Québec. The GPUs have been deployed in a hall previously used for Bitcoin mining, while mining operations continue in other halls. Datum has in turn delivered the infrastructure to its customers - including an AI coding startup and an inference platform. "AI needs clean, stable power, and Québec has it," said Romain Nouzareth, president and CEO of Sato. "We converted bitcoin mining space and handed it over to Datum 22 days after signing. That is what existing powered capacity makes possible for AI customers." Sato said the deployment is the first step in its transition toward AI compute, leveraging existing powered capacity at the company’s Joliette site. "Our customers are growing quickly, but developing new data center assets is costly and slow," said Zachary Smith, co-founder and CEO of Datum. "In Joliette, Sato was able to convert existing space to our needs in a matter of weeks, enabling us to deliver hydro-powered Nvidia B300 GPU infrastructure quickly to end users." New York-based Datum (not be confused with the UK colocation provider of the same name) is an AI cloud and network provider, founded by the co-founders of bare-metal cloud provider Packet. Using Nvidia BlueField DPUs, the company says its open network cloud lets clouds, data centers, and Edge environments connect and operate as one programmable network. The company should Datum has previously deployed network points of presence (PoPs) inside DataBank facilities in Ashburn, Dallas, and Salt Lake City. In total, the company lists availability from 16 regions globally. Founded in 2017, formerly known as Canada Computational Unlimited Corp and previously focused on cryptomining, Sato is looking to pivot towards AI compute. The company joined the TSXV in 2021. Its data center, known as Center One, launched in 2022 and is located at 289 Rue Dugas in Joliette. The facility caught fire in June 2024. As well as converting its existing cryptomine in Canada, the company also has plans to develop a 100MW campus in Gelephu Mindfulness City in Bhutan to host AI compute. The first phase will offer 5MW, and the company has said it could expand to 500MW. Launched last year, Qritical.ai is Sato’s AI cloud and GPU platform. related.title: S&P warns Nvidia credit rating could be cut over 'rising' management and governance risk

cards.body: Nvidia's credit rating could be cut by one notch over the next 90 days if the company continues to have "deficiencies" in its management and governance framework, S&P Global Ratings said in the wake of the Jensen Huang's ouster and reinstatement as Nvidia CEO. "News regarding the CEO and questions regarding potential export control violations have exposed vulnerabilities in Nvidia's management and governance framework, especially in regard to its board structure, composition, and effectiveness," S&P said in a Wednesday note. Nvidia currently holds an AA rating, the third-highest level. S&P has placed the chipmaker on "CreditWatch with negative implications," though any potential downgrade would be limited to one notch, to AA-, unless investigations or disclosures lead the agency to conclude that Nvidia's reputation or future prospects have also been harmed. A downgrade can pressure bond prices, push yields higher and raise borrowing costs. Nvidia priced $25 billion of investment-grade senior notes in June, with maturities from 2028 through 2056, shortly after S&P upgraded the company from AA- to AA. Nvidia has about $32.5 billion of bonds in the U.S. high-grade corporate bond index, according to Bloomberg. S&P's Wednesday note follows Moody's Ratings changing its outlook on Nvidia to stable from positive on Nov. 18, citing governance concerns, and leaving that outlook unchanged after Huang's return on Monday. In its note, S&P cited the "long tenure" of certain board members as a reason their independence may be "compromised" and said Nvidia's management and governance risk was "rising." The ratings agency added that it remained unaware of any remedial action taken by the board to address what could be "meaningful" management and governance deficiencies. Chairman Harvey Jones and early investor Tench Coxe have served on Nvidia's board since 1993, while Brooke Seawell joined in 1997. Mark Stevens served from 1993 to 2006 and rejoined the board in 2008. S&P also flagged questions around geopolitical risk management and internal controls arising from Nvidia's exposure to China. "While Nvidia management has delivered significant returns for its stakeholders over decades, weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning have brought questions around the "key man" risk to the forefront," S&P's Andrew Chang and David Tsui said. Chang and Tsui noted that Huang's resignation and subsequent reinstatement did not resolve questions about the board's oversight of executive conduct. The agency also intends to meet with Nvidia's board and management to discuss plans to address those deficiencies, particularly around "board independence, effective management oversight and a credible leadership succession plan." Huang returned less than two weeks after Jones said Nvidia's directors did not intend to reinstate him. cards.body: French AI cloud provider Exaion has secured a US customer under a four-year contract, while US-based AI cloud company QumulusAI has secured 2MW of colocation capacity. Under Exaion's agreement, it will provide GPU-as-a-Service in a 100 percent take-or-pay contract valued at $79 million. Exaion will provide compute powered by Nvidia HGX B300 servers for the customer. In a LinkedIn post, the company said: "Mara provides the energy-backed infrastructure, and Exaion turns it into compute and cloud services, from private cloud infrastructure to inference as a service for customers who need greater control over their data. It is also a signal of demand. Exaion’s customers and prospects have expressed demand for more than 30MW of compute capacity for delivery by the end of 2027." Mara Holdings, a digital energy and infrastructure company known for its cryptomining operations, along with EDF Pulse Ventures, acquired Exaion in August 2025. Mara is one of the biggest Bitcoin miners in the US, predominantly utilizing stranded energy assets to power modular mining units. In April 2025, the company fully energized a 25MW modular cryptomine data center powered by flared natural gas in Texas and North Dakota. In December 2024, the company acquired an onshore wind farm with plans to develop and operate a Bitcoin mining operation on the site, powered behind-the-meter. Founded in 2020, Exaion launched its first data center in Sherbrooke, Canada, in 2024. Spanning 4,000 sq ft (372 sqm), the Tier II quality facility offers 780kW of capacity. The site is home to a quantum computer from Quandela. As of February 2026, Exaion operated four data centers across Canada and France. QumulusAI secures 2MW of colocation capacity US-based AI cloud company QumulusAI, meanwhile, has signed a ten-year colocation agreement for 2MW of capacity in the northeastern US. The contract has two three-year renewal options. QumulusAI said the capacity is expected to be ready for service by the end of 2026, and the company has a right of first offer on a further 9.6MW at the site. The company is funding the first phase from cash generated by capacity already in production. “The first 2MW is scheduled for service by the end of this year, which is weeks away, not quarters,” said Michael Maniscalco, CEO of QumulusAI. “That is capacity we can put in front of customers now, with the possibility to take significantly more at the same site.” Earlier this month, QumulusAI expanded its capacity in Denver, Colorado, by 1.2MW under a five-year agreement, with automatic five-year renewal terms for the colocation capacity. It is expected to be operational from Q1 2027.

related.title: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks

cards.body: S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices. Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement. The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale. Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral. In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported. A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.

headlines.body: China’s homegrown memory comes largely from two companies, CXMT for DRAM and YMTC for 3D NAND, and both are booming. CXMT’s Oct. 30 quarterly report shows a nine-month net profit of ¥132.0 billion ($19.6 billion), against a ¥5.28 billion ($785 million) loss a year earlier, on revenue more than eight times as high, at ¥269.0 billion ($40.0 billion). YMTC’s numbers, just for Q1, are at ¥47.04 billion ($7.0 billion) in revenue and ¥33.38 billion ($5.0 billion) in profit attributable to shareholders, more than double 2025. Both are expanding and adding fabs, and each is edging into the other’s products. No Chinese manufacturer can yet produce high-bandwidth memory (HBM) in volume, though. HBM is the stacked DRAM that AI accelerators depend on, and currently the U.S. bars Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron from selling it into China. CXMT’s prospectus lists no HBM project , though its HBM3E is reportedly in risk production , an early run before the process is fully qualified. Huawei designs its own HBM but doesn’t say who makes it. Memory is a commodity, so the story is in the wafers. We cover the companies running memory fabs in China: CXMT, YMTC, a handful of smaller Chinese fabs, and Samsung and SK hynix, which run some of their biggest plants there. Huawei makes the cut for its HBM program, though it has no memory fab. Fabless designers, module makers, and NOR flash producers are left out, except XMC for its HBM line. Fab counts, products, and financials come from filings and company statements; capacities, planned fabs, and the HBM progress that remains the big question mark rest largely on anonymous reporting. Let's dive into the current state of the Chinese DRAM industry. CXMT: three DRAM fabs running, three more on the way (Image credit: CXMT) CXMT, short for ChangXin Memory Technologies, is China’s biggest homegrown DRAM maker. It operates two 12-inch fabs in Hefei and one in Beijing, each able to produce around 100,000 wafers a month. It is also building fabs in Shanghai and Hefei and is in funding talks for a second Beijing fab, which together could take it past 600,000 wafers a month. The Shanghai fab is expected to have two to three times the capacity of the Hefei base, with tools going in during the second half of 2026 and volume in 2027. CXMT is now the fourth-largest DRAM maker worldwide, with 9.5% of DRAM revenue in Q2, according to TrendForce . headlines.body: Dell Is Finally Making Money On GenAI As Traditional Servers Boom Dell ended its third quarter of fiscal 2027 with $60.2 billion with new bookings for AI servers, a backlog of these machines of $132.3 billion, and a pipeline of new orders that is many times as large as this. By Dell’s historical standards, this is absolutely ginormous. Until you realize that Dell, the largest supplier of server machinery in the world in terms of revenues and probably shipments thanks to the GenAI boom, is a mere fraction of the $2.5 trillion “cloud industry backlog” that Nvidia revealed it had when it talked about its latest financials last week. Presumably the total Nvidia backlog, which includes demand from AI model makers, enterprises, governments, and academic institutions, is even larger than $2.5 trillion. But it is probably not larger than $3 trillion to $3.5 trillion, if I have to put a number on it. Despite all of the crazy amount of money being promised for future spending on the GenAI boom, Dell is only getting a piece of the action that is proportional to its share in systems and storage overall. The good news is that Dell is getting better and better at building immense AI clusters based on Nvidia technology, and bragged in its call with Wall Street going over the Q3 F2027 numbers that it can move customers from cluster delivery to first tokens generated in a little over six hours because machines are preconfigured and pretested at the factory. This, in fact, is what is hard about scaling up production of AI clusters. You have to build a massive datacenter to test machines in the factory before you put the gear on a truck. Only a dozen companies in the world – be they original design manufacturers (ODMs) or original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) who act like ODMs sometimes – can do this at scale. But to make this all work, and result in an invoice generating event for Dell, there are some other important steps. “Behind every customer engagement and every order is a rigorous due diligence process, resulting in a fully vetted backlog,” Jeff Clarke, vice chairman and chief operating officer at Dell, explained on the call with Wall Street going over the numbers. “Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power. headlines.body: Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company faces. The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models. The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too. The U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China. Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing. Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers. When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end users of their chips are obeying the rules. However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch. And that’s why Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was such a problem for Nvidia, likely even more so than her alleged role as a source for Chinese intelligence agencies. If Nvidia personnel, from lower-level employees up to the CEO, had reason to believe that statements from Megaspeed weren’t reliable, the attorneys said, that would increase the company’s legal risk. “Government investigators likely would want to know, notwithstanding whatever formal assurances were exchanged between the parties, what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about the end use and end users of the chips,” Dan Fisher-Owens, an attorney at the firm Berliner Corcoran & Rowe, told TechCrunch last week. The concern Nvidia’s board faced when it decided to oust Huang is that he knew more about what Megaspeed was doing with Nvidia’s products than was reflected in any of the compliance statements. headlines.body: 미국 정보당국이 젠슨 황 엔비디아 최고경영자(CEO)와 불륜 관계였던 앨리스 황이 중국 정보기관 지시를 받아 스파이 활동을 했다는 증거는 없다고 의회에 보고했다는 보도가 나왔다. 월스트리트저널(WSJ)은 25일(현지시간) 이 같이 보도하며 브리핑은 도널드 트럼프 대통령이 복귀를 압박한 가운데 황 CEO가 복귀한 다음 날 열렸다고 전했다. 중앙정보국(CIA), 연방수사국(FBI), 국가정보국(DNI), 국가안보국(NSA) 당국자와 상·하원 정보위원회 위원, 양원 지도부 의원 보좌진이 참석했다. 소식통을 인용한 WSJ는 정보당국이 지금까지 확보한 증거는 두 사람 관계가 중국이 기획한 공작이 아닌 연애 관계였을 가능성을 시사한다고 전했다. 다만 새 정보가 나오면 평가가 달라질 수 있다는 지적도 나왔다. 당국자들은 중국 국가안전부가 앨리스 황에게 접근해 법적 의무라며 정보 제공을 요구했고, 앨리스 황이 관계를 이어가는 동안 접촉한 사실도 있다고 밝혔다고 WSJ는 전했다. 그러나 중요한 정보가 전달됐다는 징후는 파악되지 않았다. 남편으로 소개된 캉웨이는 국가안전부 정보원으로, 자주 접촉한 것으로 전해졌다. 정보당국은 황 CEO의 국가안보 위반 증거도 아직 없다고 통보했다. 정보당국 내 시각도 엇갈리는 것으로 알려졌다. 일부는 동기와 무관하게 정보를 조금이라도 넘겼다면 스파이라고 주장한다. 다른 쪽은 중국 기업 경영진이 보안기관 접촉을 강요받는 일이 흔해 연관성이 정황적 수준이라고 본다. 로이터통신은 트럼프 대통령의 복귀 추진 전에 법무부가 황 CEO를 공식 조사한 적이 없다고 보도했다. 토드 블랜치 법무장관은 슈퍼마이크로와 앨리스 황의 메가스피드에 대한 기존 수사를 토대로 법 위반 증거가 없다고 결론 낸 것으로 전해졌다. 추가 조사 부재는 의회의 조사 요구를 키울 전망이다. 황 CEO는 다음 주 정보위를 포함한 하원 위원회 3곳에서 비공개 면담을 하고, 상원 은행위원회 공개 청문회에도 출석한다. 권동준 기자 djkwon@etnews.com - 권동준 기자기사 더보기 - ET Events

headlines.body: Stratum Holdings and Ocean Power Technologies (OPT) have signed an agreement to explore the development of offshore data centers powered by renewable wave, wind, and solar energy. The two companies are set to begin the first phase of their joint work, looking into defined work on combining OPT’s PowerBuoy technology with Stratum’s high-performance GPU infrastructure, including Nvidia B300 GPUs. OPT's PowerBuoy is a platform that delivers renewable power and real-time data communications for remote maritime and subsea applications OPT will conduct a comprehensive technical and commercial feasibility assessment to evaluate the potential for deploying Stratum’s GPU infrastructure on its PowerBuoy platforms, including power generation and storage requirements, thermal management, communications capabilities, platform integration, and potential deployment locations. The first phase of the partnership covers feasibility and planning only, and does not include equipment fabrication, GPU integration, offshore deployment, or at-sea testing. Industries targeted by the platform include defense and security, oil and gas, environmental monitoring, and scientific exploration. “This agreement takes our collaboration with OPT from a letter of intent to defined work, with a path toward a demonstration at sea,” said Nicholas H. Adler, CEO of Stratum Holdings. “Demand for AI computing is growing faster than the power and cooling available on land, and the industry is beginning to look offshore. We believe pairing our Nvidia B300 GPUs with OPT’s PowerBuoy platform, which generates its own renewable power in a natural cooling environment, could give Stratum a differentiated position in this emerging market. The feasibility assessment is designed to give us the technical and commercial roadmap to pursue it.” “Advancing into this initial phase allows us to take a more detailed look at the technical and commercial requirements for combining our PowerBuoy technology with Stratum’s GPU infrastructure,” added Tracy Pagliara, acting president and CEO of Ocean Power Technologies. “Our focus will be on evaluating the power, thermal management, and communications capabilities necessary to support offshore AI computing and establishing a foundation for a potential demonstration program.” Stratum was formerly a real estate business and was named La Rosa Holdings Corp., but sold off its legacy real estate operations earlier this month to focus on its AI cloud business.
